subject: Hospitality
title: Ancient Roman Thermopolia
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Ancient Roman Thermopolia.

hook.text: Pompeii had over 80 thermopolia—ancient Roman fast-food counters serving hot meals to busy city dwellers.

buildup.text: Most Romans lived in tiny apartments without kitchens. Eating out wasn't luxury—it was necessity and daily routine.

discovery.text: Thermopolia served stews, lentils, fish, and wine from large clay pots embedded into stone counters—grab and go.

twist.text: Wealthy Romans looked down on thermopolia. Eating in public meant you couldn't afford a private cook at home.

climax.text: The stigma of eating out persisted for centuries. Restaurants only became respectable in 18th-century France.

punchline.text: Fast food is 2,000 years old. Rome had grab-and-go culture first.

quiz.question: Why did most Romans eat at thermopolia?
options: Their apartments had no kitchens—it was a daily necessity
